title: Can large language models predict public perceptions of support for climate action across 125 countries?
content:
Abstract
Second-order beliefs (“what people think others think”) are theorized to be a powerful driver of climate action, yet they remain costly and difficult to measure at a global scale. Here, we tested whether large language models (LLMs) can predict second-order beliefs about willingness to contribute financially to address climate change across 125 countries. In a preregistered experiment, we prompted four contemporary LLMs and benchmarked their predictions against nationally representative samples from the Gallup World Poll 2021/2022 and statistical regression models. Among the LLMs, Claude and Llama achieved the lowest average errors (∼5 and 7 percentage points, respectively). Claude's error was not statistically different from those of ordinary least squares and Lasso, whereas Llama, GPT, and Gemini performed significantly worse. Yet, accuracy depended strongly on whether prompts included each country's actual first-order willingness to act. Without it, correlations between predicted and observed second-order beliefs were close to zero across all models, even when demographic, economic, and climate information was provided. In exploratory analyses, Claude estimated first-order willingness from country-level information and used these estimates to predict second-order willingness; however, the resulting second-order predictions were unrelated to the observed values. Counterfactual and memorization checks found little evidence that the models were retrieving memorized values; the models appear mainly to map the supplied first-order value onto a second-order estimate, with little contribution from the other country-level information. Overall, the tested approach cannot substitute for survey measurement in settings where first-order data are unavailable.
